images.caption: Figure 1:Two examples of missed intent.In Case I, the reply asks whether “I’m dead” is literal when the speaker is describing a predicament. In Case II, Vidu praises the speaker for entertaining her parents’ guests but overlooks the pressure she describes. The leaderboard ranks nine systems by evidence-weighted intent fulfillmentSSand outcome qualityQQon 216 shared inputs. Times are averaged per system. For closed-source systems, timing runs from the end of user-video playback until the avatar begins speaking. For open-source systems, timing covers offline reply generation and rendering.

Figure 2:Evaluation pipeline of UUBench.(a) A user describes dance as a lifeline, and an avatar responds. (b) The speaker’s words, soft voice, lowered gaze, and upturned palms provide evidence that she seeks support and understanding. (c) Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV assesses audiovisual response quality (QQ) and how well the response addresses the needs conveyed by each applicable primitive. The latter scores are reported by dimension (x¯k\bar{x}_{k}) and combined within each response using evidence-based weights to obtain the system scoreSSafter averaging across clips.

Figure 4:Examples of user clips and digital human responses.Each case presents sampled frames and transcripts from the user and the responding system.
The examples illustrate acknowledgment of a personal experience (Case 1),
a playful reply to a recollection of being expected to perform (Case 2),
and a follow-up question prompted by a figurative expression (Case 3).
Audio delivery and temporal coordination cannot be fully assessed from static frames and transcripts alone.
